title: LFP Compression Benchmark: SVD and Adaptive SVD+WP Methods
text:
The IBL holds 936 hours of Brainwide Map (BWM) recordings and 1472 hours from the Ephys Atlas. Raw LFP at 2500 Hz, 384 channels, float32 amounts to ~12 TB for the BWM alone. After standard preprocessing (bad-channel rejection, 2–250 Hz bandpass, ×10 decimation to 250 Hz), the footprint shrinks to ~1.2 Tb — still too large for routine distribution or streaming. The goal is to identify a lossy compression strategy that reduces this further.
Practical recommendation: SVD + WP (ε≈150, α≈32) gives total CR≈125 (104-181) with RMSE≈15 µV and SNR≈10 dB. This would shrink the 936-hour BWM dataset to ~9.6 Gb.

title: LFP Compression Benchmark: SVD and Adaptive SVD+WP Methods
text:
Pre-processing pipeline
Raw LFP (NP1, 2500 Hz, .cbin) was preprocessed before benchmarking:

Bad-channel detection — channels with anomalous variance flagged and excluded.
Bandpass + CAR + decimation — 2–250 Hz FIR bandpass, common-average referencing, ×10 FIR decimation → 250 Hz float32.
Cadzow PPCA spatial denoising — F-X Cadzow on 3 s snippets (nw=64, f_max=100 Hz, max rank r=5, adaptive rank via singular-value gap threshold=2.0, PPCA outlier k=2.0) to remove incoherent channel noise.

All methods were benchmarked on the Cadzow-denoised snippets so residuals reflect compression loss, not pre-existing noise.



Cadzow denoising for PID e8f9fba4. Three 3 s snippets (rows): original / denoised (adaptive rank) / difference (same colour scale).

Adaptive WP threshold calibration
After SVD truncation at rank \(r\), each temporal component \(V_k\) (a row of \(V_r^\top\), unit-L2-norm) is wavelet-packet compressed with a per-component hard threshold:
\[\tau_k = \frac{\alpha \cdot \sigma_0}{\sigma_k}\]
where \(\sigma_0\) is the same SVD noise floor used for ε-based rank selection, \(\sigma_k\) is the singular value of component \(k\), and \(\alpha\) is a single global multiplier. The threshold ensures every discarded coefficient contributes less than \(\alpha \cdot \sigma_0\) — uniform across all components regardless of their amplitude.

Dominant components (large \(\sigma_k\)) receive a small threshold → many WP coefficients retained.
Weak components (small \(\sigma_k\)) receive a large threshold → only the coarsest WP structure kept.

\[\text{CR}_\text{total} = \text{CR}_\text{SVD} \times \text{CR}_\text{WP}, \qquad \text{CR}_\text{WP} = \frac{r \cdot n_\text{WP\,slots}}{n_\text{kept}}\]



α vs CR_WP for each SVD-stage CR (db4, level 5). Individual PIDs as thin lines; median as heavy line. Curves are tight across insertions, confirming α generalises across recordings.

NoteSVD-adapt-WP algorithm in detail





The two-stage algorithm operates on a snippet matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n_c \times n_s}\) (channels × samples):
Stage 1 — spatial compression (SVD)
\[X \approx \hat{X}_1 = U_r \, \text{diag}(s_r) \, V_r^\top\]
where \(U_r \in \mathbb{R}^{n_c \times r}\), \(s_r \in \mathbb{R}^r\), \(V_r^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times n_s}\) are the top-\(r\) singular triplets. The rank \(r\) is chosen to achieve a target CR (e.g. CR=24 → \(r \approx 12\)).
Stage 2 — temporal compression (wavelet packets)
Each of the \(r\) rows of \(V_r^\top\) is independently compressed using db4 wavelet packet decomposition (level 5). Only the top-\(f\) fraction of coefficients by magnitude are retained, giving an overall:
\[\text{CR}_{\text{total}} = \frac{n_c \, n_s}{r(n_c + n_s)} \cdot \frac{1}{f}\]
SVD-adapt (ε-sweep) selects rank automatically using:
\[\sigma_0 = \text{median}(s_{\lfloor r/2 \rfloor + 1}, \ldots, s_r), \qquad r^* = \max\{k : s_k > \varepsilon \cdot \sigma_0\}\]
Here \(\sigma_0\) is the noise-floor estimate (median of the lower half of the full singular value spectrum), and \(\varepsilon\) is a dimensionless threshold — the minimum signal-to-noise-floor ratio \(s_k / \sigma_0\) required to retain a component. Equivalently, \(\varepsilon(r) = s_r / \sigma_0\) is the \(\varepsilon\) that would select exactly rank \(r\) (as shown in the calibration figure). Sweeping \(\varepsilon\) from \(10^4\) (keep only the dominant component) down to \(10^{-1}\) (keep almost everything) traces out the full CR curve.
Reconstruction reverses the two stages: reconstruct each wavelet-compressed row, then reassemble \(\hat{X} = U_r \, \text{diag}(s_r) \, \hat{V}_r^\top\).









NoteWP coefficient selection: per-coefficient error thresholding





Setup. After SVD truncation at rank \(r\), each retained temporal component is a row \(V_k \in \mathbb{R}^{n_s}\) of \(V_r^\top\) with unit \(\ell_2\)-norm (\(\|V_k\|_2 = 1\), since \(V\) is orthonormal). The full reconstruction contribution of component \(k\) to \(X\) is \(s_k U_k V_k^\top\), whose Frobenius norm is \(s_k\).
Wavelet-packet decomposition. Each \(V_k\) is decomposed into \(n_\text{WP}\) coefficients \(\{w_{kj}\}\) via a full db4 wavelet-packet tree at level 5 (for \(n_s = 750\), \(n_\text{WP} = 960\)). Because the WP transform is orthogonal, \(\sum_j w_{kj}^2 = \|V_k\|_2^2 = 1\).
Per-component hard threshold. For each component \(k\), a threshold is set as
\[\tau_k = \frac{\alpha \cdot \sigma_0}{s_k}\]
and coefficient \(w_{kj}\) is retained only if \(|w_{kj}| \geq \tau_k\); otherwise it is set to zero:
\[\tilde{w}_{kj} = w_{kj} \cdot \mathbf{1}\!\left[|w_{kj}| \geq \tau_k\right]\]
Per-coefficient error guarantee. Zeroing \(w_{kj}\) changes the reconstruction by \(s_k \, U_k \cdot \delta v_{kj}^\top\), where \(\delta v_{kj}\) is the inverse-WP basis vector for coefficient \(j\) with unit norm. The resulting Frobenius error contribution is
\[s_k \cdot |w_{kj}| \;<\; s_k \cdot \tau_k \;=\; \alpha \cdot \sigma_0\]
Every discarded coefficient, in every component, contributes less than \(\alpha \cdot \sigma_0\) to the reconstruction error — uniformly across all ranks. This is the same absolute noise-floor reference \(\sigma_0\) used by the SVD stage, so the two thresholds speak the same language.
Compression ratio. The WP stage CR is the ratio of total available coefficient slots to those retained:
\[\text{CR}_\text{WP} = \frac{r \cdot n_\text{WP}}{\#\{(k,j) : s_k |w_{kj}| \geq \alpha\sigma_0\}}\]
Behaviour across the component spectrum.
For a component with singular value \(s_k = q \cdot \varepsilon \cdot \sigma_0\) (where \(q \geq 1\), since only components above the SVD threshold are retained), the WP threshold becomes
\[\tau_k = \frac{\alpha}{q \cdot \varepsilon}\]

Dominant components (\(q \gg 1\), \(s_k \gg \varepsilon\sigma_0\)): \(\tau_k\) is small, many WP coefficients survive — the component’s full temporal structure is preserved with only fine-scale details discarded.
Marginal components (\(q \approx 1\), \(s_k \approx \varepsilon\sigma_0\)): \(\tau_k \approx \alpha/\varepsilon\). If \(\alpha/\varepsilon\) exceeds the largest WP coefficient magnitude of \(V_k\) (empirically 0.05–0.2 for LFP), the entire component is zeroed. This is consistent behaviour: the component was weakly significant spatially and has no concentrated temporal structure, so it genuinely carries little information.

This component-level zeroing is not a design flaw — it is the natural outcome of applying a uniform per-coefficient error threshold to components with flat (noise-like) temporal spectra. In practice, at the recommended operating point (\(\varepsilon \approx 150\), \(\alpha \approx 32\), \(\alpha/\varepsilon \approx 0.21\)), components at ranks 7–13 are fully eliminated by WP, while the first 5–6 components retain 5–70% of their WP coefficients for genuine temporal compression.
Relationship to the SVD threshold. The two parameters are not independent: when \(\alpha/\varepsilon > \max_j |w_{r,j}|\) (the largest WP coefficient of the weakest retained component), WP overrides the SVD rank selection. The curves in the aggregate figure converge at high \(\alpha\) because all \(\varepsilon\) settings end up keeping the same dominant components once \(\alpha\) is large enough to purge the weaker ones. The non-redundant operating region is \(\alpha/\varepsilon \lesssim 0.1\), where WP compresses temporal structure within every kept component without discarding any of them entirely.









NoteCadzow denoising with adaptive rank and imputation





F-X Cadzow: working frequency bin by frequency bin (parameters used: nw=64, f_max=100 Hz, max rank r=5, gap_threshold=2.0, ppca_k=2.0)
This is the F-X (frequency–space) variant of Cadzow denoising, borrowed from seismic processing. Rather than applying SVD to the full time × channel matrix, the algorithm works one frequency bin at a time:

rfft the snippet → complex array \(W \in \mathbb{C}^{n_c \times n_f}\).
For each frequency bin \(f \leq f_\text{max}\), extract the spatial vector \(w_f \in \mathbb{C}^{n_c}\) (one complex amplitude per channel).
Build a block-Toeplitz trajectory matrix \(T_f\) from \(w_f\).
Compute the rank-\(r\) SVD of \(T_f\), zero the remaining singular values, and read off the denoised amplitudes.
irfft back to the time domain.

Outlier imputation (ppca_k): after the first rank-\(r\) projection, channels deviating by more than \(\text{median} + k \cdot \text{MAD}\) are replaced by their model prediction; the SVD is repeated on the cleaned data.









NotePrior context: transform methods





Before focusing on SVD variants, we benchmarked six approaches: SVD, Wavelet Packets (WP), DCT, DCT-δ, STFT, and SVD+WP. SVD consistently outperformed all transform-only methods at every compression ratio. The figure below shows the full comparison; the current analysis refines and extends only the SVD family.



Initial aggregate benchmark (11 PIDs) including all transform methods. SVD and SVD+WP dominate at every CR. DCT-δ is worst throughout.





Reconstruction gallery from initial benchmark — PID dab512bd. SVD retains spatial structure to CR=100; transform methods show block/stripe artefacts from CR=30.





Residual gallery from initial benchmark. SVD/SVD+WP residuals are spatially incoherent; DCT and STFT residuals carry structured spectral artefacts at high CR.











NotePrior-context: Gap-criterion rank selection (discarded)





We investigated an alternative rank-selection criterion based on the largest relative drop in the singular value spectrum (the “gap”):
\[r_\text{gap} = \underset{i}{\arg\max}\; \frac{s_i}{s_{i+1}} + 1\]
We also swept a gap threshold \(g\), defining rank as the last position where \(s_k / s_{k+1} \geq g\).



Gap ratio sv[k]/sv[k+1] at each rank boundary for each of the 11 PIDs. Reference lines at g=2, 5, 10.


The figure reveals why this criterion was discarded: after Cadzow denoising, the SV ratio at rank 1 is only 1.3–2.4 across all 11 PIDs — the dominant “gap” is barely larger than the secondary gaps. There is no clean separation between signal and noise in the SV ratio spectrum, so the gap threshold has very little sensitivity to the compression ratio. The ε-threshold (noise-floor-relative) criterion is far better calibrated for this data.

title: Ephys-Atlas Region Boundary Landmarks
text:
Sharp transitions in electrophysiological features at brain-region boundaries can serve as anatomical landmarks for Neuropixels probe localisation — a well-known example is the hippocampus–thalamus boundary (Benson et al. eLife 2024, Fig. 3b).
This analysis mines the IBL Ephys Atlas to discover which Cosmos-level boundaries carry the strongest, most consistent feature jumps across animals. To do so we identify which transitions we observe on our dataset by computing a transition matrix. Then we build a dataset of the features at the transitions, for each couple of transitions that has more than 32 data points. To identify which transitions are the most salient, we train a classifier to predict the transition couple from the features around the transition. We then select the 6 most salient transitions and run a feature importance SHAP analysis to understand each feature contribution.

title: Ephys-Atlas Region Boundary Landmarks
text:
Step 1 — Cosmos boundary transition matrix
For each probe, channels are depth-aggregated (modal Cosmos region), adjacent-depth transitions are counted directionally, and interior unlabelled positions are replaced by nearest-neighbour interpolation along the probe (21,435 positions replaced in vintage 2026_W24).



Directional Cosmos-level transition count matrix (vintage 2026_W24). Row = from-region, column = to-region. Colour clipped at the 97th percentile; diagonal masked.


Boundaries with ≥ 32 probe crossings in either direction are retained for downstream analyses — 18 transitions in total.

Step 3 — Dimensionality reduction (PCA)
Raw LFP features include 21 PSD-related columns (7 raw-PSD + 14 CSD-PSD) that are highly correlated due to the 1/f spectral background. Two independent PCAs compress these into 4 components:

PSD group (7 features) → psd_pc0, psd_pc1
CSD group (14 features) → csd_pc0, csd_pc1

The original PSD/CSD columns are dropped. After also removing distance_to_tip_um and the aperiodic-residual PSD features, 26 features remain for downstream analysis:

title: Ephys-Atlas Region Boundary Landmarks
text:
Step 4 — Boundary classifier

Feature vector construction
For each (probe, boundary) crossing, a difference vector is computed:
\[\mathbf{x} = \bar{\mathbf{f}}_{\text{below}} - \bar{\mathbf{f}}_{\text{above}}\]
where “below” is the from-region side (deeper) and “above” is the to-region side (shallower), each averaged over the ±1000 µm window around the crossing depth. This yields a 26-dimensional vector per sample encoding the direction and magnitude of the feature change. 1c ### Model
A Gradient Boosted classifier (HistGradientBoostingClassifier, 300 iterations) is trained on the 18-class problem using 4-fold stratified cross-validation (1,714 samples total).

title: Ephys-Atlas Region Boundary Landmarks
text:
Step 6 — Per-landmark feature importance
For each of the top-6 transitions, SHAP values (TreeExplainer on the full training set) identify which features the model relies on specifically for that boundary. Only the samples belonging to each class are used, so the result is a per-landmark fingerprint rather than a global importance ranking.



Top-10 features per landmark by mean |SHAP| value. Each panel shows one boundary (with CV accuracy); bars are colour-coded by feature group: green = LFP/CSD, purple = RMS AP / spikes / alpha, blue = waveform shape.


The per-landmark fingerprints reveal two distinct boundary types:
LFP-power boundaries — driven by psd_pc0 / csd_pc0 (broadband LFP and CSD): - TH → HPF (psd_pc0, csd_pc0, rms_ap) — broadband LFP power drop, consistent with the known DG landmark from repro-ephys. - HPF → Isocortex (csd_pc0, rms_lf_no_car, aperiodic_exponent) — CSD-dominated, reflects cortical layering. - CNU → Isocortex (psd_pc0, rms_ap, aperiodic_offset) — similar broadband + spiking signature.
Waveform-shape boundaries — driven by spike kinetics, not LFP: - HB → CB (recovery_slope, decay_fit_r_squared, cor_ratio) — purely waveform-shape; no LFP contribution. - MB → HPF (aperiodic_offset, recovery_slope, trough_time_secs) — mixed LFP + waveform. - OLF → CTXsp (recovery_time_secs, alpha_std, trough_time_secs) — waveform kinetics dominate strongly.
The clean split between LFP-power and waveform-shape landmarks suggests that different recording modalities are optimal for different anatomical boundaries — a practical guide for online landmark detection.

title: Ephys-Atlas Region Boundary Landmarks
section: Step 7 — Ceiling validation: encoding-volume virtual probes
text:
Step 7 — Ceiling validation: encoding-volume virtual probes
The measured-probe classifier tops out at ~47% because real recordings are noisy and probes are sparse. To check whether this ceiling reflects noise rather than a lack of information in the features, the same pipeline (mean-diff feature vector → GB classifier, 4-fold stratified CV) was re-run on synthetic virtual probes: a dense 200 µm AP/ML grid of vertical probes sampled directly from the brainwide encoding volume, with no real Neuropixels data involved. Because the virtual-probe grid densely covers the whole brain (including CSF/void_fluid space), it yields a broader set of 26 transitions rather than the 18 from real probes — a related but not identical label set.



Confusion matrix for the encoding-volume virtual-probe classifier — 94.5% overall accuracy, 93.8% balanced accuracy, essentially diagonal.


The noise-free volume classifier reaches 94.5% accuracy (93.8% balanced) — near-perfect, versus ~47% on real data. This confirms the measured-probe accuracy is limited by recording noise and biological variability, not by the discriminative power of the feature set or the classification method: the same features, sampled without noise, almost perfectly separate every boundary.

title: Ephys-Atlas Region Boundary Landmarks
text:
Step 8 — Depth-resolved attribution (Integrated Gradients)
SHAP (Step 6) summarises which features matter per boundary, collapsed across depth. To see where within the ±500 µm crossing window each feature matters, an MLP was trained on the full depth profile of each crossing (50 depth positions × 26 features = 1300-d input, 4-fold stratified CV) and Captum Integrated Gradients was used to attribute the prediction to every (depth, feature) pair.



Per-class Integrated Gradients heatmaps (depth × feature) for a subset of transitions. The dashed line marks the boundary (depth = 0); red/blue indicate positive/negative attribution.


The attribution maps are spatially sharp around depth 0 for the strongest landmarks (e.g. psd_pc0/csd_pc0 for TH → HPF), corroborating the SHAP fingerprints with an independent, depth-resolved method rather than a single averaged feature vector.

title: Ephys-Atlas Region Boundary Landmarks
text:
Discussion
The classification result — ~47% accuracy against a 9.3% chance level — confirms that LFP features carry strong, boundary-specific information at every well-sampled Cosmos-level interface. The top transitions (TH → HPF, HPF → Isocortex, HB → CB, CNU → Isocortex) all achieve 70–74% per-class accuracy.
The repro-ephys DG–thalamus landmark corresponds roughly to TH → HPF in Cosmos space, consistent with our finding that this is among the most reliably classified transitions. The analysis extends this to 17 additional boundaries, several of which appear even more distinctive.
The encoding-volume ceiling analysis (Step 7) shows the ~47% real-data accuracy is a noise floor, not an information floor — the same feature set reaches 94.5% when sampled without recording noise — so future gains should come from denoising / averaging across repeats rather than new features. The Integrated Gradients analysis (Step 8) independently corroborates the SHAP fingerprints with depth-resolved attributions.

Caveats

Accuracies describe generalisation across probes, not expected precision in a single experiment.
Cosmos-level regions aggregate heterogeneous substructures; finer-grained Beryl-level analysis would reveal variability within each Cosmos boundary.
Transitions involving unlabelled tissue (void, root) are biologically less interpretable — they mark where probes exit the brain rather than genuine tissue differences.
The virtual-probe ceiling analysis (Step 7) uses a broader 26-transition set than the 18 measured transitions (it includes CSF/void_fluid crossings absent from real probes), so its accuracy is not a strictly apples-to-apples upper bound on the measured-probe numbers, only a strong indication of the noise-vs-information split.



Next steps

Unsupervised SLIC supervoxel segmentation of the encoding volume is being explored as a classifier-independent check of whether boundaries emerge without any labels; not yet quantified against Cosmos boundaries.
Coronal/sagittal atlas-coverage QC panels (per-feature slices with virtual-probe overlays) have been generated to visualise where the encoding volume has real recording support vs. gaps, as a supplement to Step 5.

title: Multi-Channel LFP Denoising: NP1 vs NP2
text:
Conclusions

Voltage amplitude is equivalent between NP1 and NP2 when the same external referencing scheme is applied, once hardware filters are accounted for.
CAR can´t be applied on both NP1 and NP2, the NP2 spatial span is much shorter than NP1, resulting in a destructive effect.
First order CSD conserves a small amount of correlation, while second order CSD destroys it completely. Spatial noise attenuation slightly improves on the correlation after spatial derivative.

title: RMS bias from Common Average Referencing
text: Common Average Referencing (CAR) subtracts the mean across channels at each time step. When channels are spatially correlated this introduces a position-dependent bias in per-channel RMS: edge channels lose less variance than central ones, producing a characteristic U-shape.

title: RMS bias from Common Average Referencing
text: Common Average Referencing (CAR) subtracts the mean across channels at each time step. When channels are spatially correlated this introduces a position-dependent bias in per-channel RMS: edge channels lose less variance than central ones, producing a characteristic U-shape.

title: RMS bias from Common Average Referencing
text: Data

title: RMS bias from Common Average Referencing
text:
Model

Covariance
Consider \(N\) channels with an exponentially decaying covariance plus uncorrelated noise:
\[C_{jk} = \sigma_s^2\,e^{-|j-k|/\lambda} + \sigma_n^2\,\delta_{jk}\]
where \(\lambda\) is the spatial correlation length in channels.


Variance after CAR
The CAR-subtracted signal \(y_j = x_j - \frac{1}{N}\sum_k x_k\) has variance
\[\operatorname{Var}(y_j)
  = C_{jj}
  - \frac{2}{N}\sum_k C_{jk}
  + \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{j,k} C_{jk}\]
Setting \(r = e^{-1/\lambda}\) and splitting the absolute value, the row sum closes in a geometric series:
\[S_j \equiv \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} r^{|j-k|}
         = \frac{1 + r - r^{j+1} - r^{N-j}}{1-r}\]
The grand sum \(T \equiv \sum_j S_j\) is
\[T = \frac{N(1+r) - \dfrac{2r(1-r^N)}{1-r}}{1-r}\]
Substituting and separating the noise contribution gives the closed-form RMS profile:
\[\boxed{
  \mathrm{RMS}_j = \sqrt{
    \sigma_s^2\!\left(1 - \frac{2S_j}{N} + \frac{T}{N^2}\right)
    + \sigma_n^2\,\frac{N-1}{N}
  }
}\]
The noise term \(\sigma_n^2(N-1)/N\) is position-independent — it is the standard single-degree-of-freedom reduction from mean subtraction.


Asymptotic limits
For a channel deep in the array (\(r^j \approx 0\), \(r^{N-j} \approx 0\)):
\[S_j^\infty = \frac{1+r}{1-r} \approx 2\lambda \quad (\lambda \gg 1)\]
For an edge channel (\(j = 0\) or \(j = N-1\), with \(N \gg \lambda\)):
\[S_0 = \frac{1-r^N}{1-r} \approx \lambda\]
The edge row sum is roughly half the bulk value, so CAR removes half as much signal variance at the edges. The transition from elevated-edge to flat-bulk RMS occurs over \(\approx\lambda\) channels — the width of the U-shape horns is a direct read-out of the spatial correlation length.

title: RMS bias from Common Average Referencing
text:
Simulation


Code
import warnings
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec




Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

N = 500          # channels
T_samp = 20_000  # time samples
sigma_s = 1.0
sigma_n = 0.5
n_win = 6        # time windows for variability display

def analytical_rms(N, lam, sigma_s, sigma_n):
    """Closed-form per-channel RMS after CAR."""
    r = np.exp(-1.0 / lam)
    j = np.arange(N)
    S = (1 + r - r ** (j + 1) - r ** (N - j)) / (1 - r)
    T_grand = (N * (1 + r) - 2 * r * (1 - r**N) / (1 - r)) / (1 - r)
    var = sigma_s**2 * (1 - 2 * S / N + T_grand / N**2) + sigma_n**2 * (N - 1) / N
    return np.sqrt(np.clip(var, 0, None))

def simulate(N, lam, sigma_s, sigma_n, T_samp, rng):
    """Generate correlated data, apply CAR, return (data, data_car)."""
    idx = np.arange(N)
    C = sigma_s**2 * np.exp(-np.abs(idx[:, None] - idx[None, :]) / lam)
    C += sigma_n**2 * np.eye(N)
    evals, evecs = np.linalg.eigh(C)
    L = evecs * np.sqrt(np.maximum(evals, 0))[None, :]
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        data = L @ rng.standard_normal((N, T_samp))
    data_car = data - data.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    return data, data_car

lambdas = [100, 300]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 7), sharey="row", sharex=True)
cmap = plt.get_cmap("tab10")
win = T_samp // n_win

for col, lam in enumerate(lambdas):
    data, data_car = simulate(N, lam, sigma_s, sigma_n, T_samp, rng)
    rms_pred = analytical_rms(N, lam, sigma_s, sigma_n)

    # top row: original
    for i in range(n_win):
        s, e = i * win, (i + 1) * win
        axes[0, col].plot(np.sqrt(np.mean(data[:, s:e]**2, axis=1)),
                          color=cmap(i), alpha=0.6, lw=0.8)
    axes[0, col].set_title(f"Original  (λ = {lam})")
    axes[0, col].set_ylabel("RMS" if col == 0 else "")

    # bottom row: after CAR
    for i in range(n_win):
        s, e = i * win, (i + 1) * win
        axes[1, col].plot(np.sqrt(np.mean(data_car[:, s:e]**2, axis=1)),
                          color=cmap(i), alpha=0.6, lw=0.8)
    axes[1, col].plot(rms_pred, "k--", lw=1.5, label="Analytical")
    axes[1, col].set_title(f"After CAR  (λ = {lam})")
    axes[1, col].set_ylabel("RMS" if col == 0 else "")
    axes[1, col].set_xlabel("Channel index")
    axes[1, col].legend(fontsize=8)

fig.suptitle(
    f"N = {N}, σ_s = {sigma_s}, σ_n = {sigma_n}  —  {n_win} time windows overlaid",
    fontsize=10,
)
plt.tight_layout()
from pathlib import Path
Path("figures").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
plt.savefig("figures/simulate.png", dpi=150)
plt.close()





Per-channel RMS before and after CAR for two correlation lengths. Dashed lines are the analytical prediction.

title: RMS bias from Common Average Referencing
text:
Conclusion
CAR suppresses the spatially correlated signal most effectively for central channels — those with correlated neighbours on both sides — and least at the edges. The resulting U-shaped RMS profile is fully predicted by a closed-form expression in terms of \(r =
e^{-1/\lambda}\). Crucially, the horn width of the U directly estimates \(\lambda\): for \(\lambda = 100\) the upturn spans ~100 channels; for \(\lambda = 300\) it spans the entire 500-channel array, preventing the profile from ever flattening. This makes the post-CAR RMS a cheap diagnostic for the spatial correlation scale of the recording.
